title: Planting, soil preparation and establishment care
audience: Landscapers, planting crews and crew leaders who prepare soil, select and plant trees, shrubs and groundcovers, and provide establishment care for new plantings.
learningOutcomes: Assess a site's soil, drainage and light conditions and decide the preparation needed before planting.
Select plants that suit the site and check them against local restrictions, including declared or restricted species.
Plant to the correct depth and spacing, and protect the root zone during handling and placement.
Plan and record an establishment care period, and price planting work for its labour, materials and aftercare.

instruction.heading: Why planting succeeds or fails below ground
instruction.body: The soil may be compacted builders' fill, waterlogged clay, sand that drains too quickly, or a mix of rubble and topsoil. The drainage may send water toward a building or hold it around the roots. The site may get more sun or shade than the plant can tolerate. Preparing the site and matching the plant to it is the largest single factor in how well a planting establishes. It is also the basis for higher-value planting work, because a client who sees healthy plants after the establishment period recommends the business. Start with the site, not the plant list.

instruction.heading: Soil assessment and preparation
instruction.body: Dig a test hole in several places and look at the soil profile. Note the colour, the texture, the depth of topsoil and any layers of rubble, clay or gravel. Fill the hole with water and see how fast it drains. Feel the soil: a sandy soil falls apart in the hand, while a clay soil forms a ribbon. Test the pH and nutrient levels only if the business has a test method and the result will change the plan. Prepare the soil to suit the plants: loosen compacted ground, remove rubble, and mix in organic material where the plant needs it. Do not add large amounts of material that will create a different soil in the hole from the soil around it, because the roots will not spread. Where drainage is poor, the plan may need a raised bed or a different plant list, and that decision is recorded with the client.

instruction.heading: Selecting plants and checking restrictions
instruction.body: Select plants for the site conditions: the light, the drainage, the wind, the space available at maturity and the maintenance the client is willing to accept. Use local plant lists and native plant references where they exist for the region. Check that the plants are not declared or restricted weeds in the state or territory, and do not supply or plant a species that the local rules restrict. Check the plant's mature size against the space, the distance from buildings, services and boundaries, and the expected root spread. Where a tree is planned near a building, service or boundary, record the check and refer any question about the root zone or the tree's future height to a qualified arborist. Record the plant list with the quantities, the sizes and the source of each plant.

instruction.heading: Planting technique and handling
instruction.body: Keep the root ball intact and the plant upright from the moment it leaves the container until it is in the ground. Water the container thoroughly before removing the plant, so that the root ball holds together. Dig a hole about two to three times the width of the root ball, but no deeper than the root ball, so the plant sits on firm ground rather than loose soil. Roughen the sides of the hole if the soil is smooth and compacted, so that roots can grow out. Set the plant so that the top of the root ball sits at the same level as the surrounding soil, and check the level from two sides. Backfill with the prepared soil, firming it gently with the hands rather than stamping, and water in to settle the soil around the roots. Use mechanical aids or a team lift for large containers, and keep the lift low and close to the body to protect the back. Do not pull a plant by its stem, and do not leave the roots exposed to wind or sun while the planting continues.

instruction.heading: Establishment care, pricing and records
instruction.body: New plantings need regular water and checks until the roots spread into the surrounding soil. Write the schedule in the planting record: the watering frequency, the check dates, the mulch top-up, the pruning of damaged growth and the date for the first review. Price planting work from the labour, the materials, the soil preparation, the plant supply, the mulch and the aftercare visits. Keep the plant supply price separate from the planting labour, and explain any replacement policy in writing, without promising that every plant will survive. Keep the planting record with the plant list, the date, the preparation carried out, the mulch used and the client's sign-off.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the soil record, the plant list and the planting depth. A competent planter can show the soil test result, explain how the planting level was set, identify a plant that is too large for the space or in the wrong position, and describe the establishment care the client needs to provide. Escalate any planting near a service or building that needs a qualified check, any plant that is restricted or unidentified, any plant that is root-bound or damaged on arrival, and any request to plant in a way that conflicts with the preparation or the drainage plan.

procedure: Test the soil with a test hole and a drainage check, and record the soil type, depth of topsoil and any rubble or compaction.
Prepare the planting area to the agreed depth, loosen compacted ground and remove rubble.
Check the plant list against the site conditions, local restrictions, space at maturity and services.
Water the root ball before planting, check its condition, and remove any circling roots that the business's method allows.
Plant at the same depth as the plant was in its container, with the crown above the finished soil level.
Backfill with the prepared soil, firm it gently, and water in to remove air pockets.
Mulch the planting area with the approved mulch, keeping it clear of stems and trunks, and label the plants where useful.
Record the plant list, the planting date, the establishment care schedule and the client's sign-off.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a row of shrubs planted along a fence where the soil is compacted builders' fill with rubble, and the drainage is poor after rain.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you prepare the planting and what do you tell the client?
workedExamples.reasoning: Loosen and remove the rubble and compacted fill to the depth the plants need, and check the drainage in a test hole. If the drainage is poor, discuss a raised bed or a different plant list, and record the client's decision. Plant only after the preparation is agreed. Explain that the shrubs' growth and survival depend on the soil and the drainage, and record the establishment care schedule and the client's responsibilities.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a fast-growing tree to be planted close to the house and the side sewer line, to give shade in two years.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is this in scope, and what is recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Check the mature size and root spread against the house and the service line, and record the check. A tree close to a sewer line or a building may cause damage and needs a qualified arborist's advice on species and position. Refer the question, offer an alternative in the planting plan that suits the space, and record the client's decision. Do not plant the tree in the position requested without that check.

equipmentAndPpe: Test hole kit and soil probe
Water supply and watering can or hose with approved fitting
Gloves suitable for handling plants and soil
Eye protection when working with soil and mulch
Dust mask where dry soil or mulch is dusty
Plant labels and a planting record sheet

commonErrors.error: Planting into compacted fill or waterlogged ground without preparation.
commonErrors.prevention: Test the soil and drainage first, prepare the planting area, and agree any raised-bed or plant-list change with the client.

commonErrors.error: Planting too deep, which buries the crown and causes rot.
commonErrors.prevention: Plant at the depth the plant was growing in its container, with the crown above the finished soil level.

commonErrors.error: Choosing a plant that becomes too large for the space or sits too close to a service or building.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the mature size, the root spread and the service locations before selecting the plant.

commonErrors.error: Supplying a species that is a declared or restricted weed in the location.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the restriction list for the job location before supplying or planting any species.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Declared and restricted plant lists are set by each state, territory and local government.

Planting near services or buildings may need a qualified person's check. Tree work near power lines needs a qualified and experienced arborist and is outside this business. This lesson does not grant any arborist or tree-work licence.

Manual handling: a business must assess the risks of lifting root balls, bulk soil and mulch, and manage them as far as reasonably practicable (no date shown). Use mechanical aids and team lifts where needed.
Soil and mulch can carry biological hazards and dust.

qualityStandard: The soil and drainage check is recorded before any plant is selected or placed.
Each plant is checked against the site, the space at maturity, the services and the local restriction list.
Every plant is planted at the correct depth, with the root zone protected and watered in.
The establishment care schedule is written and given to the client, and the client has confirmed it.
documentationEvidence: Soil and drainage check record with the photographs taken with consent.
Plant list with quantities, sizes, sources and the restriction check.
Planting record with the date, the preparation carried out and the mulch used.
Establishment care schedule and client confirmation.
summary: Test the soil and drainage before choosing plants, and prepare the planting area to suit.
Check each plant against the site, its mature size, the services and the local restriction list.
Plant at the correct depth, backfill firmly, water in and mulch clear of stems.
Agree an establishment care schedule in writing, and price the planting for labour, materials and aftercare.

knowledgeChecks.question: A planting area is compacted builders' fill with rubble and poor drainage. What should happen before planting?
options: Plant straight away, since the plants will adapt to the soil over time and the drainage will improve once the roots spread
Test the soil and drainage, prepare the area, and agree any raised-bed or plant-list change with the client before planting.
Add a large amount of fertiliser to the planting hole and continue, since the fertiliser will fix the soil

knowledgeChecks.question: At what depth should a shrub be planted?
options: Deeper than its container depth, so the roots are well covered and the plant feels secure
With the crown buried under mulch to protect it from the sun and the wind during the first year
At the same depth it was growing in its container, with the crown above the finished soil level.

knowledgeChecks.question: The client asks for a fast-growing tree close to the house and a sewer line. What is the correct response?
options: Check its mature size and root spread against the house and service, and refer the question to a qualified arborist before planting.
Plant it where requested, since the client has chosen the spot and the crew should follow that choice without any further question
Plant it and cut the roots if they cause a problem later, since that is easy to do on the day after the planting is finished
